Subject: GPU queue throttling observed (Dedicated pool) — impact to Atlas Analytics

Hi Carlos —

Wanted to let you know we observed a period of elevated queuing and token throttling that affected your dedicated GPU pool this morning (approx 05:40–06:20 UTC). Our telemetry shows an increase in long-running generation tasks that caused local autoscaler signals to trigger conservative throttling to preserve SLOs across the pool.

Immediate impact we saw for Atlas: higher median tail latency (95th pct) for generation routes and occasional request rejections for bursty jobs. No model data was lost and your VPC/data plane remained isolated.

What we did immediately:
- Increased headroom on your dedicated allocation to clear the backlog (06:05 UTC).
- Disabled a conservatively tuned autoscale rule that was over-reacting to transient queue length.
- Applied a temporary per-tenant queue cap to prevent repeated re-entry to throttling while we finish the root-cause work.

Next steps we will take this week:
1) Deliver a short incident timeline and proposed remediation plan (I’ve attached a timeline PDF).
2) Share a draft postmortem and remediation items by EOD Friday (we’ll invite you to a 30-min review call).
3) Recommend a short-term config change for your workload (adjusted burst policy + KV cache parameters) — we’ll include the exact config and rollout window.

We know this is impactful and I’m sorry for the disruption. We’ll propose a credit for the affected window once the final scope is confirmed.

Are you available for a review call tomorrow (June 5) at 15:00 UTC? If not, suggest an alternate time and we’ll adjust.

Thanks,
Marissa

Subject: RE: GPU queue throttling observed — quick technical summary

Quick technical notes for the thread (so Marissa can reply with specifics):

What happened (summary):
- A recent autoscaler tweak (rolled out in canary last week) changed the aggressiveness of the backpressure trigger threshold. For highly bursty tenant workloads (Atlas’s nightly RL fine-tuning jobs), queued KV memory and job runtime variance produced repeated upscales then conservative throttles.
- The autoscaler interpreted the queue spike as a global load signal and started applying tenant-protect throttles across the pool (safeguard to protect SLAs for all tenants).

Immediate fix applied (06:05–06:12 UTC):
- We reverted the canary change in the autoscaler for dedicated pools (rollback 06:05).
- Manually increased pool headroom and rotated one NVLink host to take in-flight KV cache to speed cache warmups (06:08).
- Applied temporary per-tenant request cap to prevent queue amplification while headroom increased.

Scope:
- Affected requests: approx 0.9% of Atlas’s token volume across the 40-min window; 2% of requests saw >2x latency spikes; <0.1% returned explicit rate rejections.
- No data integrity or model versioning issues.

Planned remediation (short list):
1) Harden autoscaler rule with workload-aware smoothing (W-24).
2) Add tenant-level anomaly detection to avoid global pool throttle for single-tenant spikes (W-48).
3) Publish a set of recommended burst policies for Dedicated customers.

I’ll draft a short postmortem and add telemetry graphs.

—Jonas
SRE Lead — Serving Runtime

Hi Carlos / Miguel —

Thanks for the quick reply and for looping Miguel in. Short answers:
- ETA for normal latency: we globally restored headroom and the transient throttling cleared by ~06:20 UTC. We’ve been monitoring since and median latencies are back to baseline, tail spikes reduced but we’ll continue to watch for 72 hours.
- Batch jobs: none were dropped. Some jobs experienced longer run durations and a handful were retried by your job orchestrator; we did not force requeues or drop any jobs on our side.

I’ve attached the incident timeline and a draft postmortem for your review. Proposed customer steps (optional):
- Lower your short-term concurrency cap by 10% for scheduled nightly fine-tuning windows OR switch to the recommended burst profile we attach.

We’d like to schedule a 30-minute review on Jun 5 at 15:00 UTC (I've tentatively booked this — invite forthcoming). If that doesn’t work, tell us a preferred window and we’ll move it.

Regarding credits: we will calculate a proportional credit for the affected window and share details after the postmortem scope is finalized.

Regards,
Marissa

Subject: Dedicated GPU pool — postmortem & remediation tracker (Atlas Analytics incident)

Folks —

Finalized notes from our internal postmortem and remediation tracker (customer-facing summary sent on Jun 4; we’re closing internal items now). Key points:

Root cause: An over-aggressive autoscaler rule (canary) combined with high-variance, long-running tenant jobs. The rule caused global tenant-protect throttling that amplified queue length.

Timeline highlights:
- 05:36 UTC: sudden queue growth observed for pool 7a.
- 05:40 UTC: first customer-reported latency anomalies (Atlas monitoring).
- 06:05 UTC: rollback of autoscaler canary and headroom increase.
- 06:20 UTC: throttling subsided; monitoring resumed.

Customer impact summary: approx 0.9% token volume affected for Atlas; minimal request rejects; no data loss.

Remediation actions (owner — due):
- Harden autoscaler smoothing and add rollback test in canary pipeline (Jonas — due 2026-06-18).
- Implement tenant-level anomaly detection (Sean — due 2026-07-02).
- Publish Dedicated burst / concurrency best-practices + add to onboarding docs (Marissa — due 2026-06-11).
- Run post-deploy soak test against production-like burst patterns (Infra — due 2026-06-25).

Customer communications: we proposed a proportional credit; Marissa will finalize credit calculation and confirm with Finance by Jun 12.

Attached: mitigation-runbook.pdf (runbook for on-call to clear queue amplifications) and the customer-facing postmortem draft.

Thanks team — please update the tracker with progress on your items.

—Monica
Head of Infra Reliability — Redwood Inference
